paper_title: MT Forcing: Towards Stable and Consistent Multi-Turn Image Editing with Autoregressive Diffusion

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Multi-turn image editing aims to modify an image according to a sequence of instructions, enabling more effective interactive visual content creation for users. However, existing methods often exhibit noticeable drift after only a few editing turns, manifesting in two aspects: 1) unstable visual quality, with accumulating artifacts and degraded details; and 2) inconsistent image content, with unintended changes to preserved regions and prior edits. To address these challenges, we propose MT Forcing, a novel training paradigm for multi-turn image editing with unified multimodal models (UMMs) based on autoregressive diffusion. Specifically, we propose Single-Turn Distribution Matching Distillation (Single-Turn DMD), which supervises student self-rollouts with a teacher that applies cumulative edits to the source image in a single turn, providing visual-quality guidance without recursive error accumulation. Additionally, we introduce Teacher-Forcing Guidance, which supervises history-dependent transitions on reference trajectories during warmup and as a regularizer during distillation, encouraging cross-turn content consistency beyond what per-turn distribution matching alone can ensure. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach significantly improves the multi-turn image editing capabilities of UMMs, yielding more stable visual quality and stronger cross-turn consistency.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Multi-turn image editing [28, 40, 61, 92, 112] aims to progressively modify an image through sequence of user instructions. With rapid advances in unified multimodal models (UMMs) [12, 15, 67], this task has attracted growing attention from the research community. Compared with conventional single-turn editing [3, 10, 30, 36, 57, 68, 100], it enables users to continuously refine visual content as their creative intentions evolve, making it well suited to creative workflows requiring precise control over successive edits. Since each edit builds on the results of prior turns, multi-turn image editing is inherently causal [62, 86], which naturally aligns with autoregressive (AR) diffusion [13, 19, 23, 37] in UMMs. Such design enables later edits to draw on the accumulated interaction history while responding to new user instructions. However, existing methods often exhibit drift after only few editing turns (see Fig. 1 for examples), manifesting in two aspects: 1) unstable visual quality, with accumulating visual artifacts and progressive degradation of fine-grained textures and local structures; and 2) inconsistent image content, with unintended alterations to regions outside the requested edit and failures to retain prior edits that should remain unchanged. We attribute these failures to exposure bias [60, 66], arising from the mismatch between training and inference conditions. During training, the model typically conditions on reference histories, whereas inference requires recursively conditioning on its own imperfect histories. To overcome these challenges, we propose MT Forcing, training paradigm for UMMs based on AR diffusion that enables stable and consistent multi-turn image editing. First, we introduce Single-Turn Distribution Matching Distillation (Single-Turn DMD) to counteract visual-quality drift across editing turns. Our design follows two observations: 1) single editing turn typically introduces limited degradation [72]; and 2) editing models can execute multiple actions in one turn [73] (see Fig. 3). These observations motivate using single-turn editing quality as the reference for every turn of multi-turn student. Specifically, we reorganize all instructions up to the current turn into bundled prompt that expresses their cumulative editing intent as single edit to the source image. Conditioned on this prompt and the source image, the teacher executes the accumulated edits in one turn, providing quality reference without cross-turn error accumulation. The student performs autoregressive self-rollouts during training [1, 29], conditioning each edit on its own imperfect outputs. At each turn, DMD loss [16, 44, 94, 95] aligns the students rollout output distribution with the teachers single-turn output distribution for the same cumulative editing intent. This trains the student to maintain visual quality under the histories encountered during inference, mitigating exposure bias and progressive visual degradation. However, the bundled prompt specifies cumulative editing intent without fixing the visual details established in preceding student outputs (see Fig. 4), so per-turn distribution matching alone does not guarantee cross-turn consistency. To improve cross-turn consistency, we introduce Teacher-Forcing Guidance, which trains the student with teacher forcing on consistent reference trajectories [27, 31, 99]. We apply this teacher-forced supervision in two stages. 1) Teacher-Forcing Warmup: before Single-Turn DMD training, we perform supervised fine-tuning to teach the model to produce consistent edits conditioned on coherent reference histories. 2) Teacher-Forcing Regularization: during Single-Turn DMD training, we retain this supervision with lower weight as regularizer to preserve history-dependent behavior and cross-turn consistency during distillation [7, 78, 97]. Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate that MT Forcing achieves more stable visual quality, greater content consistency, and better instruction following across successive editing turns. To evaluate multi-turn image editing comprehensively, we build on MTEdit-Benchs [6] assessment of instruction following, content consistency, and visual quality. We additionally introduce Pixel, metric based on image matching [24] that measures geometric alignment between successive editing outputs. MT Forcing also achieves better alignment under this metric, providing additional evidence of improved content preservation across turns. In summary, we 1) propose Single-Turn DMD to stabilize visual quality across editing turns by aligning student rollouts with single-turn teacher; 2) introduce Teacher-Forcing Guidance to preserve cross-turn content consistency through teacher-forced training on consistent reference trajectories; and 3) combine these complementary objectives into MT Forcing, which achieves more stable visual quality, greater content consistency, and better instruction following in extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Multi-Turn Image Editing extends instruction-based image editing [3, 26, 35, 46, 70, 73, 75, 79] to an interactive setting, where users progressively refine an image through sequence of instructions. straightforward approach is to recursively apply single-turn editor, conditioning each turn on the previous output and the current instruction [28, 40, 101, 112]. However, this formulation does not explicitly model the full interaction history, limiting its ability to 2 retain earlier constraints and resolve context-dependent instructions [91]. Recent approaches build on UMMs to incorporate previous instructions and generated images into shared context for subsequent edits [12, 92]. Multi-turn Consistent Image Editing [112] uses flow-based inversion and dual-objective guidance to stabilize sampling, while FreqEdit [40] preserves high-frequency features to reduce accumulated degradation. VINCIE [62] learns in-context editing from video-derived image-text sequences, and AnchorEdit [86] introduces causal self-rollout training and memory to preserve subject identity across turns. MT-EditFlow [28] optimizes rewards aggregated over editing trajectories, while Edit-R2 [92] reconstructs session intent and jointly optimizes reasoning and image generation. Most recently, MT-OPSD [101] constructs degraded inputs through identity rollouts and distills clean-conditioned teacher predictions into the student. However, the mismatch between training on reference histories and inference on self-generated outputs can cause errors to accumulate, making visual quality and content consistency difficult to maintain over successive turns [28, 101]. Diffusion Distillation aims to reduce iterative diffusion sampling to one or few steps with minimal loss in generation quality. Teacher-trajectory regression learns the teachers sampling dynamics through direct noise-toimage regression [51, 106] or progressive step compression [58, 63], while InstaFlow [47] straightens trajectories to facilitate one-step distillation. Consistency-based methods constrain predictions along diffusion trajectory to share common endpoint [53, 54, 71], with extensions to interval mappings [25, 33, 77, 107] and transitive or bootstrapped supervision [2, 22]. Continuous-time formulations improve scalability [48], while rCM [109] combines consistency distillation with score regularization. Distribution-level methods supervise generated samples through adversarial objectives [32, 41, 64, 65, 87] or score-based matching [55, 59, 111]. DMD [95] matches distributions using the difference between target and student-distribution scores, while DMD2 [94] stabilizes online score estimation and incorporates adversarial supervision. Subsequent work improves distillation quality and scalability [11, 20, 49, 110], refines multi-step matching and guidance [16, 44, 81], and explores alternative divergence objectives [88]. Auxiliary student-score estimation can also be replaced by generator-derived surrogates [34] or discriminative density-ratio estimation [98]. We use DMD2 to transfer single-turn editing quality to outputs under imperfect multi-turn histories. Autoregressive Diffusion generates visual content in causal autoregressive manner. For images, UMMs [12, 14, 15, 18, 21, 67, 82, 83] extend sequence modeling to visual understanding, generation, and editing, often combining autoregressive context modeling with diffusion-based image synthesis. For videos, common strategy distills pretrained bidirectional diffusion models into few-step autoregressive generators, reducing latency and enabling streaming beyond the training clip length [29, 96]. CausVid [96] uses asymmetric distribution matching between bidirectional teacher and causal student. Diffusion Forcing [5] trains with independently noised sequence elements, whereas Self Forcing [29] trains on autoregressive self-rollouts to align training with inference. Other studies improve causal student initialization [108, 113] and scalable few-step or one-step distillation [17, 102]. Long-horizon stability is further strengthened through streaming training and error control [4, 9, 38, 45, 90, 114], long-range context modeling [8, 85, 89], and KV-cache management [52, 69, 93, 104]. Further work improves distillation quality and diversity [50, 105] and reduces inference costs through sparse or multi-scale attention [39, 56, 84]. However, directly transferring these methods to multi-turn image editing is challenging, as bidirectional teachers capable of jointly generating complete editing trajectories are unavailable.

Sec. 3.1 defines the multi-turn editing problem and its traininginference mismatch. Sec. 3.2 introduces Single-Turn DMD to supervise student rollouts with single-turn teacher. Sec. 3.3 presents Teacher-Forcing Guidance for cross-turn consistency. Algorithm 1 summarizes the overall training procedure.

sections.title: 3.2 Single-Turn Distribution Matching Distillation
sections.content: Recent video-generation methods [9, 29] mitigate rollout drift by distilling from pretrained bidirectional teachers that jointly model multiple frames. Multi-turn editing lacks corresponding bidirectional UMM that jointly generates instruction-conditioned editing trajectories. We therefore propose Single-Turn DMD, in which single-turn editing teacher supervises each generated turn; we next specify its conditioning and training signal. At turn i, we reorganize all editing instructions up to that turn, c1:i, into single-turn editing prompt, termed the bundled prompt ci = Reorganize(c1:i). This prompt expresses the cumulative editing intent as one edit to be applied directly to the source image. For example, add vase followed by make it blue can be reorganized as add blue vase. sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: For baselines, we evaluate MT Forcing on two UMMs: SenseNova-U1 [15] and SenseNova-U1.5 [14]. We compare each editors performance with and without MT Forcing. Ablation studies use SenseNova-U1.5 [14] as the baseline. For benchmarking, we evaluate on the step-wise sub-bench of MTEdit-Bench [6], which contains 100 sessions, each comprising source image and eight sequential editing instructions. For metrics, we follow MTEdit-Bench [6] and report Instruction Following (IF), Content Consistency (CC), and Drift Robustness Score (DRS). IF measures fulfillment of the current instruction, while CC evaluates preservation of the intended cumulative content under all instructions up to the current turn. Both are scored from 0 to 10 by Qwen3.5-Plus [74]. DRS measures robustness against visual-quality drift across turns, computed as the mean of the VisualQuality-R1 [80] and RALI [103] scores, and ranges from 0 to 5. Higher values indicate better performance for all three metrics. Moreover, we introduce Pixel to quantify geometric alignment between successive editing outputs. Using MatchAnything-RoMa [24], we compute the mean matched-point displacement in pixels as Pixeli = Mi1 (cid:80) v2, where Mi contains valid matches between xi1 and xi, with x0 = xsrc. sections.title: 4.2 Main Results
sections.content: Quantitative comparison. Table 1 shows that MT Forcing outperforms both base editors on all four metrics from Turn 4 onward, with increasingly pronounced gains in IF, CC, and DRS at later turns. At Turn 8, IF and CC improve by 7.45 and 6.82 on SenseNova-U1, and by 4.65 and 4.46 on SenseNova-U1.5, respectively. On SenseNova-U1.5, MT Forcing maintains DRS between 4.20 and 4.35 throughout the session, while the baseline declines from 4.09 to 3.03. Its eight-turn mean Pixel also decreases from 6.34 to 0.74, an 88.4% reduction in matched-point displacement. Qualitative comparison. Fig. 5 compares SenseNova-U1 and SenseNova-U1.5 with their MT Forcing counterparts at Turns 1, 4, and 8. By Turn 8, the baselines exhibit oversaturated lighting and harsh textures in the car scene, and speckled snow and exaggerated contrast in the mountain scene. MT Forcing preserves cleaner textures and coherent scene structure across turns while retaining earlier edits, including the red car body, roof box, tent, skis, and marker post. These examples visually support the improved drift robustness and content consistency measured in Table 1. 7 Figure 6. Qualitative ablation of MT Forcing. SenseNova-U1.5 is compared with Single-Turn DMD only, Teacher-Forcing Guidance only, and the full method at Turns 4 and 8. Enlarged crops highlight differences in texture detail.

sections.title: 4.3 Ablation Studies
sections.content: Table 2 and Fig. 6 compare the pretrained baseline, Single-Turn DMD only, Teacher-Forcing Guidance only, and full MT Forcing. The DMD-only variant initializes all three models from the pretrained editor and omits reference supervision. The guidance-only variant uses teacher-forcing warmup followed by continued reference supervision, without DMD. The full method combines warmup with DMD and teacherforcing regularization. We further investigate the teacher-forcing regularization weight λTF  (Fig. 7)  . Table 2. Component ablation of MT Forcing. Eight-turn mean scores on SenseNova-U1.5 for the step-wise sub-bench of MTEdit-Bench. The full method performs best across all four metrics. Single-Turn DMD Teacher-Forcing Guidance IF 8.47 9.02 9.10 9.66 CC 7.09 7.64 7.83 8.40 DRS Pixel 3.83 4.12 3.92 4.30 6.34 2.51 2. 0.74 Ablation of the two components. Table 2 shows that either Single-Turn DMD or Teacher-Forcing Guidance alone improves all four metrics over the pretrained baseline, while combining them yields the best results: 9.66 IF, 8.40 CC, 4.30 DRS, and 0.74 Pixel. The qualitative comparison in Fig. 6 reveals their complementary roles. DMD alone improves visual quality by reducing the baselines exaggerated textures, but cross-turn content inconsistency remains evident: the enlarged wood-grain patterns change between Turns 4 and 8. Teacher-Forcing Guidance alone benefits from supervised fine-tuning on consistent reference trajectories, but training on reference histories does not address exposure bias under self-generated histories. Consequently, visual-quality degradation persists, with harsh wood-grain textures and excessive contrast at Turn 8. Full MT Forcing combines distribution matching on student rollouts with reference supervision, preserving more consistent wood-grain structure and clearer local details across turns. Together, the quantitative and qualitative results support the complementary benefits of the two components for visual-quality stability and cross-turn consistency. Effect of the regularization weight. The teacher-forcing regularization weight λTF controls the balance between reference supervision for consistency and rollout distribution matching for visual quality. Fig. 7 compares weights of 1, 0.5, 0.25, and 0.1. Larger weights introduce visible blur: at 1 and 0.5, the huskys fur appears smooth, and individual strands are difficult to distinguish in the enlarged crops. Reducing the weight to 0.25 or 0.1 restores finer fur detail and sharper coat boundaries, offering favorable balance between content consistency and visual clarity. 8 Figure 7. Visual quality comparison under different regularization weights. From left to right: the source image and outputs with λTF = 1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.1. Enlarged crops show differences in fur detail.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented MT Forcing, which combines learning on self-generated histories with reference supervision for stable and consistent multi-turn image editing with autoregressive UMMs. Single-Turn DMD transfers single-turn editing quality to student rollouts using teacher that realizes cumulative editing intent directly from the source image, avoiding recursive error accumulation in its supervision. Teacher-Forcing Guidance complements marginal distribution matching with reference-conditioned supervision during warmup and distillation, encouraging the historyoutput dependencies needed for content preservation. Experiments on SenseNova-U1 and SenseNova-U1.5 demonstrate improved instruction following, content consistency, and drift robustness on the eight-turn step-wise sub-bench of MTEdit-Bench, with increasingly pronounced benefits at later turns.
